1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 {Black chooses The Nimzo-Indian Defense, 
favorite of many strong players after 3.Nc3. Other possibilities are 3. 
d5, leading to the Queen's Gambit Declined and 3. c5, leading to the 
Benoni Defense after 4.d5 exd5 5.cxd5 d6. The 3. Bb4 variation was 
introduced by a great player of the past Aaron Nimzowitch. Originally, the
idea was to stop e2-e4 and play Bxc3, damaging White pawns on the 
Queenside. Later, other plans interesting ideas were developed.} 4.e3 {By 
far the most popular. Also possible 4.Nf3, 4.a3, 4.f3 and 4.Bg5.} 4...O-O 
{Black makes no secret of his plans. More flexible is 4. ... c5, 
immediately attacking the center.} 5.Bd3 d5 {Otherwise by playing 6.e4 
White will grab all the space in the center.} 6.Nf3 b6 
    ( 6...Nbd7 {is another possibility, that after} 7.a3 dxc4 8.Bxc4 Bd6 
    9.b4 e5 10.Bb2 a5 11.b5 exd4 12.Nxd4 Nb6 13.Be2 {this leads to a small
    edge for White according to Botvinnik.} )
7.O-O Bb7 8.cxd5 {Since e3-e4 is very unlikely, White decided to ease the 
tension in the center and go for a so-called Pillsberry attack. The 
maneuver of a Knight to e5, supported by f2-f4 and followed by a rook-lift
was introduced in similar positions by a great American player of late 
19th century, Garry Nelson Pillsberry.} 8...exd5 
    ( {In case of} 8...Nxd5 {White plays} 9.Qc2 {attacking h7, and after} 
    9...h6 10.e4! {grabs the center and the initiative.} )
9.Ne5 a6 
    ( {Black's last move is known to the chess theory, but I fail to see 
    the point of it. Instead} 9...Bd6 {makes sence. After} 10.f4 c5 11.Qf3
    Nc6 12.Bd2 cxd4 13.Nxc6 Bxc6 14.exd4 Re8 15.Rae1 Qc7 {Black had an 
    even game in Knaak - Lukacs, Leipzig, 1986.} )
10.Bd2 
    ( {In Donner - van Scheltinga, Beverwijk, 1965, White played} 10.Ne2 {
    and had no advantage after} 10...Bd6 11.b3 Nbd7 12.Bb2 Re8 13.f4 Ne4 )
10...Bd6 11.f4 c5 
    ( {The "Pillsberry Knight" is being successfully installed. Black must
    start some counterplay in the center. In case of} 11...Ne4 {White 
    plays} 12.Nxe4 dxe4 13.Bc4 {and the pressure against f7 is very 
    unpleasant. Black can play} 13...Bxe5 {but after} 14.fxe5 {the opening
    of the f-file makes things only worse.} )
12.Rf3 {White starts a dangerous attack on the Kingnside.} 12...Nc6 
    ( {Nc6 allows the following sacrifice, but in case of} 12...Ne4 13.Rh3
    {threatens Qd1-h5, White keeps a dangerous attack. For instance:} 
    13...Bc8? 14.Nxe4! Bxh3 15.Ng5 {and White threatens Bxh7+ as well as 
    Nxh3.} )
13.Nxd5!? 
    ( 13.Rh3 {didn't promise much after} 13...h6 14.Rg3 cxd4 15.Nxc6 Bxc6 
    16.exd4 Ne4 {and Black has a good position, thanks to the outpost e4.}
    )
13...Bxe5 {The only move.} 
    ( {In case of} 13...Nxd5? 14.Bxh7+ Kxh7 
        ( 14...Kh8 15.Rh3 +- )
    15.Rh3+ Kg8 16.Qh5 +- {Black gets checkmated.} )
14.Nxf6+ Bxf6 {What now?} 15.Bxh7+! Kxh7 16.Rh3+ Kg8 17.Qh5 {White 
threatens a checkmate and Black has only one defense.} 17...Bh4 18.Rxh4 f6
{Black escaped a checkmate, but White has two pawns for a piece and an 
ongoing attack.} 19.d5 Ne7 
    ( {As was pointed out by IM John Donaldson in "Inside Chess" magazine,
    attempt} 19...Nd4 20.exd4 Qxd5 {meets} 21.Qh7+ Kf7 22.Rg4 {and after} 
    22...Qxd4+ 23.Kh1 Rg8 24.Bc3 {White keeps a winning attack.} )
20.e4 Nxd5? 
    ( {Black could play} 20...Qe8! {and I failed to find win after} 21.
    Qh7+ Kf7 22.Rh6! {(threatening Rxf6+ and Bc3+)} 22...Rg8 23.Bc3 Kf8 {
    and now} 24.Bxf6? gxh6 25.Qxh6+ Kf7 -/+ {wins for Black.} )
    ( {Donaldson also recommends} 20...Bxd5! {and concludes that White 
    must give perpetual check:} 21.Qh7+ Kf7 22.Qh5+ Kg8 = )
21.Rd1!! {A fantastic reply. Such move is easy to miss.} 21...Nc7 22.Bc3 
Qe7 23.e5! Rad8 24.Re1! {A remarkable sequence of moves from White. Now 
every piece is involved in the attack and Black is defenseless. Black 
tries to keep the position closed.} 24...f5 25.Qh7+ Kf7 26.e6+! {This 
little sacrifice finishes Black off. Opening of the e-file plus an attack 
on g7 make Black's position hopeless.} 26...Nxe6 27.Bxg7 Ke8 28.Bxf8! {The
most simple solution.} 28...Qxh7 29.Rxe6+ Kd7 30.Rd6+ 1-0

Kasparov starts a remarkable plan.} 
    ( {Theory is} 7...cxd4 8.Nxd4 Bg7 )
8.d5 Bxc3+ 9.bxc3 Na5 10.O-O 
    ( 10.Nd2!? {will become a novelty in Rublevsky - Ehlvest, Polanica 
    Zdroj 1997.} )
10...f6 
    ( 10...Nxc4!? 11.Qe2 Nb6 12.c4 {looks suspicious for Black.} )
11.Nd2 b6 {Black can ignore the development, because the centre is closed.
} 12.Qe2 Qa4 13.f4 Nh6 14.e5!? {White cannot create an attack.} 14...O-O-O
15.Rb1!? Nf5!? 16.g4?! {White weakens his pawn structure.} 16...Nh4?! 
    ( 16...Ng7! 17.Re1 h5! {brings a positional advantage for Black.} )
17.exf6 exf6 18.Qf2 g5 19.Ne4 Qe8!? 
    ( {The tactical line} 19...h5! 20.gxh5 Qxc4 21.Nxf6 Rdf8! 22.fxg5 Rxf6
    ! 23.Bf4! Rxf4 24.Qxf4 Qxf4 25.Rxf4 Rxh5 26.Kh1 Ng6 27.Rf7 {leads to 
    chances for both sides.} )
20.Re1! Qg6 21.fxg5 
    ( 21.f5!? Qg7! 22.Ng3 Nxc4 23.Nh5 Qf7 24.Re6 Ne5 25.Qe2! Rhe8 26.Qe4 {
    will be regarded as a chance for White by Shirov, but} 26...Rxe6! 27.
    dxe6 d5! 28.Qxe5 Qxh5 29.Qe2 Qe8 30.Qa6+ Kb8 31.Rxb6+ axb6 32.Qxb6+ {
    leads to perpetual check.} )
21...Rhe8! 22.Nxd6+! Rxd6 23.Rxe8+ Qxe8 24.Bf4! Nxc4! 25.Bxd6 Nd2! {Garry 
finds a brilliant draw.} 26.Rd1 Qe4!! 27.Bg3 {Russia defeated Spain, 
because Bareev won.} 
    ( 27.Rxd2 Qb1+ 28.Qf1 Nf3+ 29.Kg2 Qxf1+ 30.Kxf1 Nxd2+ {(Shirov)} 31.
    Ke1! Ne4 32.Bf8! fxg5 {draws as well.} )
    ( 27.Bg3 Nhf3+ 28.Kh1 Ne1+ 29.Kg1 Nef3+ {delivers a repetition.} )
